Measuring the tool in 3D

I get $10,000 worth of measurements from a $40 drawing tablet. Now I want the height of the pen too.

My SO-101 draws with a pen held in its gripper. A controller turns the path I ask for into motor commands, and the motors report their joint angles back. So where is the pen tip? You'd think you could push those angles through the arm's geometry and read off the answer. The trouble is that every encoder sits at a joint. The links bend between joints and the pen holder flexes, so joint angles alone leave part of the nib's motion unmeasured. I want to compare two controllers, carry the corrections I learn while drawing over to moves in the air, and fit a model of how this arm really moves. For all three I need an observer outside the arm that watches the nib in x, y and z.

The cheapest observer is a drawing tablet, and on paper it's surprisingly good: a Wacom Intuos S costs about $40 and quotes ±0.25 mm. The catch is height. In the clip under the board, the arm spends 12 s coming down to the tablet and 12 s leaving it, and for most of that time the tablet can't place the tip. To get the third dimension you have to track a different point, a target on the gripper, and work out where the nib must be. So how much error do we introduce by watching the gripper instead of the nib? Let's start with the distance between them.

Read panel 5 as a ladder. Sweeping stations offer room-sized coverage, reported up to 10 × 10 m with four stations, and in that study tracking error grew with tool speed. With optical capture, several cameras watch markers fixed to the gripper and combine their views to locate it 240 times a second. That's useful, but now we have cameras to mount and calibrate around the arm. The laser tracker measures a reflector's position independently of the arm. At 1 m its specified error limit is ±0.021 mm, about 12 times tighter than the tablet's ±0.25 mm tolerance, though the two are different kinds of specification. None of these numbers is the accuracy you would get at the nib of this arm: each comes from its own setup, reference point, processing and metric, which is why the board names the metric next to every value.

So for a small arm I'd run two instruments together. The tablet covers everything where the pen touches paper. A calibrated phone camera with a ChArUco target covers the moves in the air, with the target close to the nib on a stiff holder. For anything more expensive, I'd start with the move the cheaper setup can't measure and the point on the arm I actually need to track. Does the target disappear from view? Do the samples arrive too late? Then ask whether the new system fixes that problem, and what the mounts, host, calibration, frame registration and software add on top of the component prices.
